strengths: Well-motivated contribution addressing a genuine limitation of prior work—no existing method can handle multiple NeRF architectures
Sound technical approach combining GMN encoders with rendering and contrastive losses; parameter graph representation is principled
Comprehensive ablation studies clearly demonstrating that rendering loss (LR) alone creates architecture-specific clusters while contrastive loss (LC) enables architecture-agnosticism
Robust experimental evaluation including classification, retrieval, and analysis of unseen architectural variants (MLP-2L, TRI-16W, etc.)
First framework to process NeRF architectures unseen at training time, showing non-trivial generalization
Clear presentation with informative visualizations (Figure 3 t-SNE plots effectively illustrate latent space organization)
Good reproducibility with implementation details in appendix and reliance on released codebases
weaknesses: Severely limited architectural scope—evaluation restricted to only 2 base architectures (MLP, tri-plane); 'unseen' variants are minor modifications (different layer counts/dimensions), not fundamentally different designs; critical gap given paper claims to handle modern NeRF architectures
Weak instance-level retrieval performance (Table 5: ~29% recall@1, ~70% recall@10) contradicts the core promise of architecture-agnostic matching; paper acknowledges this is 'far from being solved'

Negligible performance improvement in natural multi-architecture setting—Table 1 shows 93.5% (multi-arch) vs. 92.1-93.1% (single-arch baselines); advantage only appears in artificial cross-architecture scenarios
Evaluation limited to synthetic ShapeNet data (13 object classes, clean settings); no validation on real-world NeRFs with complex geometry, lighting, or scenes
Dependence on paired training data (same object, different architectures) is a practical limitation not adequately discussed; unclear how scalable or feasible this is in real scenarios
Missing computational cost analysis—no comparison of inference time or total cost versus baselines; unclear if flexibility justifies computational overhead
No hyperparameter sensitivity analysis; λ = 2e-2 appears arbitrarily chosen to balance loss magnitudes; robustness unknown
Contrastive loss contribution somewhat overshadowed by reliance on existing GMN (Lim et al. 2024) and decoder (nf2vec) architectures; main novelty is combining and evaluating on NeRFs
Title claim 'Embed Any NeRF' overstated given evaluation on only 2 base architectures and absence of state-of-the-art designs (hash tables, etc.) acknowledged by authors

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Addresses the real limitation that prior work (nf2vec, Cardace et al.) can only handle specific NeRF architectures, which is relevant given constant evolution of NeRF designs

Sound technical approach: Parameter graph representation from Lim et al. is appropriate for the problem; the motivation for combining rendering loss (semantic content) with contrastive loss (architecture invariance) is well-reasoned

Comprehensive experimental design within scope: Multiple settings (single/multi-architecture), ablation studies (LR/LR+C/LC), latent space analysis (t-SNE), and downstream tasks (classification/retrieval)
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with effective figures (Figure 1-2) that clearly communicate the approach and problem setup

Insightful loss analysis: Figure 3 effectively demonstrates that LR alone creates architecture-based subclusters while LC creates architecture-agnostic clusters, providing useful insight into trade-offs
Good implementation details: Appendix provides sufficient architectural and hyperparameter details for reproducibility
weaknesses: Critical scope limitation: Experiments only use two base NeRF architectures (MLP and tri-plane) from existing work that the authors explicitly acknowledge as 'not state-of-the-art.' Hash table methods (Instant-NGP, Zip-NeRF) are mentioned as routinely used by practitioners but not evaluated. This fundamentally undermines the main claim about architecture-agnosticism

Incremental technical contribution: Combines existing components (GMN from Lim et al. 2024, decoder from nf2vec, SigLIP loss from Zhai et al. 2023) with minimal novel technical development. The main contribution is identifying that this combination works, but the individual pieces are not novel

Method requires manual graph conversion: Despite claims of being 'architecture-agnostic,' the approach still requires converting each architecture to a parameter graph representation. The paper doesn't discuss failure modes, architectural constraints, or how to handle architectures with complex weight sharing patterns

Weak instance-level retrieval results: Table 5 shows only 29% recall@1 for the best method (LC), rising to 70.7% at recall@10. Authors acknowledge 'the task is challenging and far from being solved.' This is problematic since instance-level retrieval best demonstrates architecture-agnosticism—yet performs poorly

Inconsistent generalization to unseen architectures: Table 3 shows highly variable performance (e.g., TRI-16W: 7% vs MLP-2L: 91.8%). The paper identifies patterns (e.g., 'changing tri-plane hyperparameters is most disruptive') but provides no principled framework for predicting performance on truly new architectures

LR+C fails to achieve full architecture-agnosticism: Figure 3 (middle) shows that LR+C still produces architecture-based sub-clusters for some classes (airplane, car). The paper acknowledges this represents a trade-off rather than a solution, contradicting the main narrative

Limited experimental scope: All experiments on synthetic ShapeNetRender (13 object classes). No evaluation on real-world scenes, complex NeRF applications, or truly different architectural paradigms. 'Unseen' architectures are minor variations (different layer counts/dimensions)

Modest improvements over baselines: Single-architecture comparison (Table 2) shows only ~1-2% improvement over nf2vec/Cardace et al. Multi-architecture setting has no comparison since baselines cannot operate in this setting

Theoretical justification lacking: Why should contrastive pairs of same-object NeRFs lead to architecture-agnostic embeddings? The mechanism is not theoretically analyzed, only empirically observed. No discussion of when/why this might fail
Missing ablations: No ablation on λ=2e-2 (chosen to equalize loss magnitudes), other hyperparameters, or architectural choices in the GMN

Incomplete latent space analysis: Paper doesn't explain why some architectures generalize well (MLP-2L) while others fail catastrophically (TRI-16W). This is critical for understanding the method's limitations

strengths: First architecture-agnostic framework for processing NeRFs with arbitrary designs, addressing a genuine limitation of prior methods (nf2vec, Cardace et al.)

Important empirical discovery that contrastive loss (LC) is necessary to create architecture-agnostic embeddings, while rendering loss (LR) alone creates architecture-dependent clusters (well-illustrated in Figure 3)
Sound technical approach combining GMNs with appropriate parameter graph representations and principled dual loss objectives
Comprehensive experimental design including multi-architecture, single-architecture, and unseen architecture settings with systematic ablations (LR, LR+C, LC)
Demonstrates generalization to unseen architectural variants (MLP-2L, MLP-32H, etc.) without explicit training
Well-written paper with clear presentation, good visualizations, and detailed appendices enabling reproducibility
Thorough evaluation across classification and retrieval tasks with both quantitative metrics and qualitative results
weaknesses: Severely limited architecture coverage: experiments validate only 2 base NeRF types (MLP, tri-plane), both not state-of-the-art. No evaluation on modern hash-based NeRFs (Instant-NGP, Zip-NeRF). 'Unseen architectures' are minor hyperparameter variations, not fundamentally different designs. Claim of handling 'arbitrary NeRF architectures' is significantly overstated.

Modest and inconsistent performance improvements: single-architecture gains are marginal (93.6% vs 92.1% for MLP), and LR+C actually reduces multi-architecture classification accuracy (91.9% vs 93.5% for LR). Instance-level retrieval is weak (29% recall@1), undermining the core benefit of architecture-agnostic processing.

Limited experimental scope restricted to synthetic ShapeNetRender (13 classes). No evaluation on real-world scenes or larger-scale NeRF datasets (ScanNeRF, LLFF, Blender). Results may not generalize beyond small object representations.

Incomplete baseline comparisons for multi-architecture setting since prior methods cannot process both architectures. No exploration of alternative approaches (e.g., training separate models with fusion strategies).

Instance-level retrieval (most important for multi-architecture setting) shows weak performance: only 29-45% recall@1 indicates true matches are often not top results, limiting practical applicability
Limited hyperparameter analysis: λ balancing factor chosen ad-hoc with only one value tested. No ablation on GMN architecture choices or contrastive loss initialization parameters.
Scalability concerns unaddressed: 2-4 week training times reported, single GPU only, no analysis of computational complexity or memory requirements for large networks
Theoretical understanding limited: minimal explanation of why contrastive learning specifically solves architecture-agnosticity or how the method scales to drastically different architectures

strengths: First framework to handle diverse NeRF architectures (MLPs, tri-planes, hash tables) in unified setting—clear novel contribution
Technically sound method combining Graph Meta-Networks with contrastive learning (SigLIP), well-motivated by latent space analysis
Comprehensive single-dataset evaluation: 13 architectures, multiple settings (seen/unseen), both classification and retrieval tasks, good ablations
Novel parameter graph representation for hash tables with proven memory efficiency (O(N(T+F)) vs naive O(N(R³+F)))
Excellent ablation study (Section 4.1, Figure 3) clearly demonstrating why contrastive loss is necessary for architecture invariance
Outperforms single-architecture baselines (nf2vec, Cardace et al.) where comparisons possible (Table 3)
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, builds on published codebases
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: all training and most evaluation restricted to ShapenetRender (13 synthetic classes); only one qualitative Objaverse experiment—critical limitation for generalization claims
Unseen architectures are only hyperparameter variations within seen families; no evaluation on truly novel NeRF designs or architectures requiring new graph conversions

Modest empirical results: retrieval recall@10 maxes at 72.7% (Table 6); cross-architecture classification drops dramatically (93.6%→25.3%, Table 2); hash table sub-clustering persists even in best case
Incomplete loss function justification: λ=2×10⁻² only justified by similar magnitudes with no ablation; SigLIP hyperparameters (t=10, b=-10) not validated for NeRF context
Hash table graph representation lacks empirical validation that proposed O(N(T+F)) design is optimal compared to alternatives
Insufficient analysis of failure cases: HASH-11T particularly challenging and TRI-16W show anomalies without explanation; qualitative failures (television in Figure 8) not analyzed
No quantitative cross-dataset evaluation despite critical importance; no inference timing comparisons; computational efficiency unclear (2 weeks training)
Limited latent space interpretability: unclear what semantic features are captured; no visualization of learned representations or feature analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a real limitation of prior work (architecture-specific methods)
Technically sound approach with principled parameter graph representation for hash tables
Comprehensive experimental breadth across 13 architectures and multiple task types
Insightful latent space analysis (Section 4.1, Figure 3) showing why contrastive loss is necessary
Clear presentation with extensive appendices and implementation details
First work to apply weight space processing to hash-table parameterized NeRFs
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily combines existing components (GMN from Lim et al., SigLIP from Zhai et al., nf2vec decoder) with hash table conversion being an incremental extension
Severely restricted experimental scope: all training/testing on single synthetic dataset (ShapenetRender) with only 13 object classes; acknowledged limitation in conclusion
Weak practical results in key tasks: retrieval recall@10 only 27.2% for ALL/ALL (Table 6), classification on unseen architectures drops to 24.5%-72.1% (Table 4), nearly random for 13-class problem
Misleading 'unseen architectures' framing: only hyperparameter variations within known families, not true out-of-distribution generalization; no test on fundamentally different NeRF variants
Hash table sub-clustering not resolved: Figure 3 shows hash tables form separate sub-clusters despite LR+C, contradicting 'architecture-agnostic' claims
Marginal single-architecture improvements: MLP 93.6% vs nf2vec 92.1% (+1.5%), TRI 94.0% vs Cardace et al. 93.1% (+0.9%); improvements within noise
Limited Objaverse generalization validation: only qualitative retrieval results (Figs 4, 8) showing failure cases; no quantitative cross-dataset evaluation
Incomplete ablations: no sensitivity analysis on λ, no alternatives to SigLIP, no batch size studies despite known SigLIP sensitivity
Task-dependent loss selection: LR vs LR+C choice requires knowing evaluation scenario; suggests combined loss doesn't properly balance objectives
Incomplete failure analysis: HASH-11T and TRI-16W underperformance not investigated; paper only acknowledges without explanation

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem addressing real limitations of prior work (nf2vec, Cardace et al.) that are restricted to specific NeRF architectures
Sound technical contributions including memory-efficient parameter graph conversion for hash tables and insightful analysis of why rendering loss alone fails
Comprehensive experimental evaluation on 13 diverse architectures with thorough ablations demonstrating the necessity of combining rendering and contrastive losses
First framework to handle downstream tasks on NeRF weight-space representations with hash table architectures, which are now the most widely adopted in practice
Strong single-architecture classification results exceeding prior baselines (93.6% vs 92.1% for MLP; 94.0% vs 93.1% for TRI)
Clear presentation with excellent latent space analysis (Figure 3) providing intuition for design choices and good reproducibility details
Demonstrates effective generalization to unseen architectural variations within known families and includes cross-dataset evaluation (ObjaNeRF)
weaknesses: Limited to single dataset (ShapenetRender with 13 classes) for primary evaluation; only one cross-dataset experiment (ObjaNeRF) using the same architecture family seen in training, substantially constraining generalizability claims

Weak instance-level retrieval performance with very low recall@k metrics (5.3% for ALL/ALL, 13-14% for cross-architecture pairs in Table 6) despite presentation as a main contribution; limited investigation into why retrieval is substantially harder than classification

Conservative scope of 'unseen architectures'—all tested variations remain within the same architecture family (e.g., same MLP+triplane structure with different hyperparameters); no true cross-family generalization demonstrated

Significant performance degradation on certain architectural variations (HASH-11T: 24.5% vs HASH-3N: 88.3%) suggesting brittleness; limited analysis of why specific variations are particularly challenging

Missing ablations on loss hyperparameter λ (only 2×10⁻² tested) and decoder design choices; unclear how well the nf2vec decoder (designed for MLPs) generalizes to fundamentally different NeRF parameterizations (tri-planes, hash tables)

Incomplete baseline comparisons—cannot directly compare on multi-architecture tasks, and some single-architecture comparisons are missing or potentially incomparable due to different experimental protocols
Limited interpretability analysis of what the encoder learns about different architectures and insufficient investigation of failure cases (e.g., why certain architectural variations fail)
Retrieval evaluation uses only recall@k metric; lacks other standard IR metrics (mAP, NDCG) and statistical significance testing
